# On the Architecture of Wonder: Why We Build Cathedrals We'll Never See Completed

There's a particular kind of hope embedded in the act of planting a tree you'll never sit beneath, of beginning work that extends beyond your lifetime. This is different from faith—it's something quieter, more practical, yet somehow more audacious. It's the impulse that built Chartres Cathedral over nearly two centuries, that drove the Japanese to design gardens meant to mature 300 years after their designers' deaths, that makes a person renovate a house they're already planning to leave.

I've been thinking about this lately, especially in an age that prizes efficiency, immediate returns, and the quantifiable impact of individual effort. We live in a culture obsessed with disruption and innovation—the quick pivots, the exit strategies, the quarterly earnings calls. And yet something in us rebels against this velocity. Something in us wants to build slowly, to contribute to something larger than ourselves, to participate in projects whose full beauty we'll never witness.

My grandfather was a carpenter. Not a famous one—he built houses in a small Pennsylvania town, nothing that would ever make an architectural magazine. He died at seventy-two, and I inherited a small wooden box filled with his hand planes, their wooden handles worn smooth from decades of use. These tools are beautiful in a way that's hard to explain to someone who doesn't work with their hands. The patina isn't the result of stylistic choice; it's the honest record of use, of thousands of hours spent shaping wood.

When I hold these planes, I think about the houses he built, many of which still stand. I've walked past some of them over the years. They're ordinary houses—three bedrooms, maybe, simple pitched roofs, nothing extraordinary. But they're solid. They've weathered sixty years of Pennsylvania winters. They shelter families who had nothing to do with my grandfather's decision to join the carpenter's union, to learn his craft, to apply himself with integrity.

Did he expect to be remembered through his tools? Did he imagine someone—his grandson—holding his planes and wondering about the houses they built? I don't think he thought about it much. He was solving the problem in front of him: how to build a house that would last, that would shelter people, that would be worth the work it demanded. The immortality was incidental.

But that incidental quality is exactly what I want to explore. We've become so conscious of legacy, so aware of how every action might be "remembered" or "go viral," that we've lost track of what made the best work so durable in the first place: the fact that it wasn't built for remembrance. It was built because it needed to be built, because it was the right thing to make, because the work itself demanded excellence.

There's a medieval term I love: *ad maiorem Dei gloriam*—for the greater glory of God. It's what motivated the craftsmen who carved intricate details into the undersides of pews, places no one would ever see. The ornament was there not for human praise but for the integrity of the whole. The cathedral was being built for God, allegedly, but really it was being built for its own sake, so that whoever encountered it—a century later, three centuries later—would experience something true about human aspiration and capability.

I think about this in our current moment, when so much of what we make is designed to be consumed immediately and discarded. We're drowning in products engineered for obsolescence, in content designed to trigger engagement rather than understanding, in buildings that will be demolished before their mortgages are paid off. The speed is dizzying.

And yet there are pockets of resistance. I've noticed them everywhere, once you start looking. There are people who apprentice for years to learn how to make Japanese swords or hand-forge tools or restore medieval illuminated manuscripts. There are urban farmers who've planted perennial food forests knowing they'll take years to mature. There are programmers building open-source software that no one will pay them for, creating tools that will outlive them, benefit people they'll never meet.

What motivates these people? Not hope of fame, certainly. Not economic reward. It's something closer to love—love of the craft itself, love of making something true, love of being part of a conversation that stretches across centuries.

I read recently about the Sagrada Familia in Barcelona. Gaudí took over the project in 1883 and worked on it until his death in 1926. He famously didn't expect to see it completed. When asked about the slow pace, he reportedly said: "My client is not in a hurry." His client was God, and he meant it both literally (this was a religious man) and metaphorically (the work itself was the point, not its completion).

The cathedral still isn't finished, over a century after his death. And instead of being a failure, this has become part of its power. The ongoing construction is an act of humility, an acknowledgment that some things are bigger than any individual life. The scaffolding is part of the structure. The work continues, carried forward by people who knew neither Gaudí nor the original architects, but who understand that they're custodians of something that matters.

This is almost incomprehensible in a startup culture. The entire business model depends on completing the arc: found company, achieve growth, exit. The longer something takes, the less viable it becomes. We measure success in speed. Move fast and break things, as they say, and somehow the "breaking things" part has been gradually erased from the equation.

But I wonder if we've miscalculated what speed actually costs us. When everything is optimized for rapid iteration and quick returns, we lose the capacity for deep work—for understanding something so thoroughly that you can contribute to its improvement across decades. We lose the ability to plant trees for our grandchildren. We lose the very possibility of becoming masters, because mastery requires a kind of commitment that a career of disruption doesn't permit.

I have a friend who's spent the last fifteen years learning to repair old typewriters. Not because there's a market for it. The opposite—typewriters are supposedly obsolete. But she loves them, loves the mechanical ingenuity of them, loves the relationship that develops between a person and a particular machine. She has customers who came to her with their grandfather's typewriter, the one he typed his novel on in 1962, and she brings it back to life. It's beautiful work. It's utterly impractical. It's absolutely necessary.

There's a passage in a Robert Pirsig book about the concept of quality—the idea that if you're doing something, you might as well do it well, for its own sake. Not because anyone's watching, not because it will be monetized or celebrated, but because quality is inherently satisfying to the person performing the work. It's an answer to meaninglessness. If nothing else, I can make this well. I can contribute something true to the world, something it didn't have before.

The cathedrals of the Middle Ages were built by people who would never see them completed. The masons who laid the foundation stones knew they were working on behalf of people not yet born. It wasn't a sacrifice—it was an honor. To be part of something that would outlive you, to make something that would shelter generations you'd never meet: that was achievement.

We've lost access to that kind of meaning, I think. We've been told that meaning comes from individual achievement, from disruption, from being first or being famous. But these are shallow sources of meaning. They're exhausting to chase. The real satisfaction comes from participating in something larger than yourself, from doing work that matters regardless of whether you're recognized for it, from building things whose full impact you'll never witness.

I don't know what my grandfather would have made of all this—of my attempt to derive meaning from his hand planes, to fashion a narrative of quiet integrity from his ordinary professional life. He probably would have just suggested I fix something with one of the planes if I wanted to understand them. That's the kind of person he was—action over reflection, results over philosophy.

But maybe that's exactly the point. The philosophy that matters most isn't the kind you write or speak. It's the philosophy embedded in how you do your work, in the choices you make about quality when no one's watching, in the decision to contribute to something you won't see completed because it's the right contribution to make.

There's a cathedral being built in our age, even if we can't see it clearly. It's not made of stone. It's made of code written to solve real problems, of art created to change how we see, of relationships tended with care, of knowledge preserved and transmitted to those who come after. Every person who chooses to do their work well, who takes on the apprenticeship required to develop mastery, who plants something with faith that others will tend it—they're all adding to that cathedral.

And that, I think, is the architecture of hope: not confidence that you'll see the results, but willingness to contribute your part anyway. Not certainty of legacy, but commitment to excellence regardless. It's radical, in its quiet way. It's the opposite of the culture of speed. And it might be the only way back to work that actually means something.
